title: A pricing page for a fintech product
metaTitle: A fintech product pricing page that shows fit
excerpt: A fintech pricing page should show what is included, what is not, and the shape of the price, then offer a way to open an account or talk to sales.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground, a clear span for a page that has to show the shape of a price.
caption: A valley, a river, and a tree line. The price should be this easy to trace. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a fintech pricing page list exact numbers?
faqs.answer: List exact numbers when they are true for the buyer you are addressing. When the number depends on volume, country, or risk, show the shape instead: a platform fee, a per-transaction fee, a percentage, a floor. A page that says "contact us" and nothing else makes the buyer do the work the page was supposed to do.

faqs.question: What belongs in the included and not-included lists?
faqs.answer: Included means the things a buyer would assume are in the price and might be wrong about. Not included means the things that surprise people later: FX, chargebacks, expedited payouts, implementation, a second entity. Write both lists in the buyer's words. A feature name from the internal roadmap is not an inclusion.

faqs.question: How many pricing tiers should the page have?
faqs.answer: As many as you can explain without a footnote that changes the meaning. Two honest paths, self-serve and a conversation, are often enough. Four tiers with overlapping bullets teach the buyer that the differences are decorative. If a tier exists only so the middle one looks reasonable, remove it.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A fintech product pricing page is where a buyer who may move money decides whether they fit, not where they do arithmetic. Show what is included, what is not, and the shape of the price. Then show how to start an account or talk to sales.

Do not hide that shape if the buyer will ask anyway. A blank "custom" card with a form under it is a delay, not a strategy. The page should leave a careful person able to say what they would pay for, and what they would not.

## Judge fit before you ask for math

People do not come to a pricing page to enjoy a table. They come to answer a smaller question. Am I the kind of customer this product is built for, and is the cost in a range I can take to someone else? If the page opens with a slogan about flexible plans, it has postponed the answer.

Nielsen Norman Group's work on page visits notes that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they actually open. A pricing page that buries the fee under three paragraphs of positioning will be read as a blur. Put the shape where a scan can find it. The prose can explain. It should not be the only place the number lives.

Write the page for the buyer who is already slightly skeptical. They have been on other sites that said "transparent pricing" and then revealed a setup fee in a contract. Your job is to be the page that does not do that. Name the unit. Per account, per payout, per month, per country. A percentage with no unit is not a price.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether someone will leave feeling they need to search again to get better information. A pricing page that forces a second search, or a sales call, just to learn the shape of the fee fails that test. The call can still be the right next step for a large account. It should not be the only way to learn whether a small one is in range.

## What is included

Inclusion is a promise about the job, not a dump of feature names. Group it by what the buyer is trying to finish.

A useful included list for a money product often covers four kinds of things:

- The core movement of money: the payout, the collection, the card, the ledger entry.
- The account around it: users, roles, statements, exports.
- The support that comes with the fee: hours, a named channel, a review of exceptions.
- The implementation that is in the price, if any of it is.

Write each line so a person outside the company can tell whether they get it. "Dashboard access" is weak. "Two admin seats and a read-only export of every payout" is a line someone can accept or reject. "Priority support" is weak. "A reply from a person on business days, with after-hours coverage for failed payouts" is a line they can plan around.

If a tier includes something another tier does not, say the difference in the same words on both cards. Do not make the reader reconstruct the matrix by toggling a monthly and yearly switch. The switch can exist. The difference should still be readable in one glance.

## What is not included

The not-included list is where trust is won or lost. Buyers who have been surprised before will look for it. If you do not write it, they will assume the surprise is hiding.

Name the common extras in plain language. Foreign exchange. Chargebacks. Expedited settlement. A second legal entity. Onboarding that requires your engineers. A dedicated environment. Printed checks. Cash. Countries you do not serve. Anything your sales team currently explains on the second call belongs on this list if it changes the fit.

Keep the tone flat. A not-included line is not an apology and not a joke. "We do not hold customer funds; a partner bank does" is a boundary. "Unlimited everything" is a line you will have to walk back. Boundaries make the included list believable. A page with fifteen inclusions and zero limits reads like a draft.

Put the limits next to the plan they affect. A footnote that applies to every card, parked under a logo row, will be missed. Nielsen's quarter-of-the-text finding is a reason to repeat a limit in the card itself, in short words, rather than hoping the reader reaches the legal block.

## The shape of the price

Show the shape even when you cannot show a single number. Shape means the parts and how they combine.

Examples of a shape, written as a founder might actually charge:

- A monthly platform fee, plus a fee per successful payout.
- A percentage of volume, with a monthly minimum.
- A flat fee for the software, and a separate schedule for money movement.
- A quote, because risk and country change the price, with the inputs you will ask for.

Pick the one that is true. Do not publish a low anchor that no real customer pays. A "$0 to start" line that requires a paid implementation before any money moves is a different product. Say that.

If you have a self-serve number and a sales number, label the buyers. "Teams moving under this volume" and "teams with multiple entities" are labels. "Starter" and "Enterprise," with the same six bullets and a darker button, are not. The name of the tier should tell a person whether to keep reading.

Currency and billing period belong in the same glance as the figure. A monthly price shown next to an annual toggle that quietly changes the meaning is how people lose the thread. State the period in the label. If annual billing is a discount, say the discount. Do not make the reader multiply.

## Fees a careful buyer will hunt for

On a money product, the headline price is rarely the whole price. The page should answer the hunt before it starts. You do not need every schedule. You need the lines that change a yes into a no.

Write short answers for the questions you already hear:

- Is there a fee when a payout fails, or only when it succeeds?
- Who pays the card network fee, you or the customer?
- Is foreign exchange a spread, a listed rate, or a separate invoice?
- Are refunds and chargebacks priced differently from the original payment?
- Is there a fee to close the account or to export the history?

If the honest answer is "it depends," say what it depends on. Volume, corridor, card type, risk tier. Then say where the schedule lives, or that sales will send it before a contract. "It depends" alone sends the reader back to a search box. Google's people-first test is relevant on a financial topic, where trust carries extra weight. A reader should leave knowing the next fact, not hunting for it on a forum.

Do not invent precision you do not have. A range you can stand behind is better than a single number your next contract will contradict. If a fee is regulated or set by a partner, say who sets it. The buyer is trying to understand responsibility, not only cost.

## The next step on the same page

Every plan needs a next step that matches the plan. A self-serve price should open an account, and the line beside the button should say what the application asks for. A sales price should book a conversation, and the line should say what to bring. Volume, countries, and whether you already move money somewhere else are enough. A ten-field form on the pricing page is a way to lose the person you just convinced.

Use the same verbs you use on the homepage. If the homepage says "Open an account," this page should not switch to "Get started" without a reason. Consistency is how a buyer knows they are still in the same decision.

One path can be an email only when a conversation is the real product and a calendar is the wrong tool. Say what happens after they write. Who replies, and what you will ask. A mailto link with no sentence is a dead end. Most fintech teams are better off with a short form that leads to a person, or a direct way to open the account, than with a menu of contact methods.

## How to test the page with a skeptical reader

Hand the page to someone who knows the product only from the outside. Ask them to say, in one minute, who the price is for, what they get, what they do not get, and what they would do next. If they start calculating before they can answer those four, the hierarchy is wrong. If they say they would need to "talk to someone to find out anything," the shape is still hidden.

Then read the page against your last five sales conversations. Every surprise you had to explain is a candidate for the not-included list or the fee hunt. Every question you answered with "it is on the site" should actually be on the site, in the card, not in a PDF linked from the footer.

Keep the page shorter than the contract. The contract can be precise. The page can be the map of that precision. When a line needs a lawyer, link the policy and keep the summary in ordinary words. A pricing page written entirely in defined terms is a document. Buyers do not decide fit inside a document on the first visit.

After the price is legible, the buyer still needs to know what work you actually do. [The services page a fintech product actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-fintech-product-actually-needs) is the next piece: each offer in the buyer's language, with an outcome, a boundary, and a next step.
